lessons.title: Measuring and Marking Out Metal
lessons.body:
Before you cut, drill, or bend any metal, you must measure and mark it accurately. In tool making, a mistake of 2 mm can mean a wasted piece of steel. Start with a steel rule (300 mm or 600 mm) and a scriberâa sharp, hardened steel pin with a point. For agricultural tools like hoe blades or mower parts, you often work from a drawing or a sample. Place your metal on a flat surface, like a steel plate or a heavy bench. Use a try square to check that edges are straight and at 90 degrees. If the edge is rough, file it first.

To mark a line, apply layout dye (or chalk, or even a permanent marker) to the metal. This makes scribed lines visible. Hold the steel rule firmly against the edge, and scribe a line by pulling the scriber onceâdo not go back and forth. For circles, use a pair of dividers or a trammel. Set the distance between the points to the radius you need. For example, to mark a 10 mm hole, set dividers to 5 mm. Place the fixed point at the center punch mark, then swing the dividers to scratch the circle.

Center punching is critical. A center punch is a hardened steel rod with a pointed tip. Place the punch on your intersection mark, hold it vertical, and hit it once with a hammer (1 kg to 2 kg). This creates a small dent that guides your drill bit later. For accurate work, use an automatic center punchâit has a spring inside and you just press down.

Always double-check your measurements before cutting. Use a caliper or micrometer for precise work. A vernier caliper can measure to 0.02 mm. For most agricultural tools, Â±0.5 mm is acceptable. Remember: measure twice, cut once. In rural workshops, where replacing metal is costly, this rule saves time and money.

Finally, keep your marking tools clean and dry. Rust on a scriber or rule ruins accuracy. Store them in a wooden box or cloth roll. Practice on scrap metal until you can scribe a straight line and punch a center mark without slipping.

lessons.title: Cutting Metal with Hacksaws and Shears
lessons.body:
Cutting metal is a core skill for making tools. You will use a hacksaw for thick bars and pipes, and tin snips or shears for thin sheet metal. Start with a hacksaw: it has a frame and a blade with 14, 18, or 24 teeth per inch (TPI). For general work on mild steel, use 18 TPI. For thin-walled pipe or sheet, use 24 TPI to avoid snagging. For thick solid bar, use 14 TPI.

Mount your work in a bench vise. Mark your cut line with a scriber and center punch. Start the cut by drawing the saw backward a few times to make a groove. Then use full strokes, pushing forward and pulling back. Apply light pressure on the forward stroke only. Let the saw do the workâpushing too hard breaks teeth. Keep the blade lubricated with a few drops of engine oil or water. A good cut should take 30 to 60 seconds for a 25 mm steel bar.

If the blade wanders, don't twist it. Stop, reposition the saw in the groove, and continue. For long cuts, rotate the blade 90 degrees in the frame to cut deeper. When you are almost through, slow down and support the offcut to prevent it from falling and bending the blade.

For sheet metal up to 1.5 mm thick, use tin snips. There are straight, left-cutting, and right-cutting snips. For straight cuts, use straight snips. For curves, use left or right snips depending on the direction. Mark your line, then clamp the sheet to a bench. Start at an edge and cut with short, firm strokes. Do not close the snips completelyâthis creates a jagged edge. For thicker sheet (up to 2 mm), use a bench shear or a nibbler.

Always wear gloves and safety glasses. Cut edges are razor-sharp. After cutting, file the edges to remove burrs. In African workshops, a hacksaw and a pair of good snips are often the only cutting tools available, so master them. Practice on scrap metal until your cuts are straight and square.

lessons.title: Filing and Shaping Metal Edges
lessons.body:
After cutting, metal edges are rough and sharp. Filing removes burrs, squares edges, and shapes curves. You need a set of files: a flat file for straight edges, a half-round for curves, and a round file for holes. For mild steel, use a single-cut file for finishing and a double-cut file for rapid removal. File lengths range from 100 mm to 300 mm. Start with a 200 mm bastard cut file for general work.

Secure your work in a vise at about elbow height. Hold the file with one hand on the handle and the other on the tip. For flat filing, push the file forward and slightly down, using the full length of the file. Apply pressure on the forward stroke only; lift the file on the return. Do not rock the fileâkeep it flat. For draw filing (finishing), hold the file at 90 degrees to the edge and push it sideways. This produces a smooth surface.

To square an edge, file until the edge is flat and at 90 degrees to the face. Check with a try square. For curved shapes, use a half-round file. Clamp the work so the curve is accessible. File with a rocking motion, following the curve. For holes, use a round file. Turn the file slightly as you push.

File cards (wire brushes) clean the file teeth. Clogged files scratch instead of cut. Clean your file every few minutes. Chalk on the file reduces clogging when filing soft metals like aluminum.

For agricultural tools, filing is used to sharpen hoe blades, machetes, and axes. A sharp edge is a filed edge. But for tool making, filing is for shaping and fitting. After filing, deburr all edges. A smooth edge prevents cuts and improves fit. In rural Africa, a good file can last years if kept dry and clean. Store files separately to avoid dulling. Practice on scrap steel until you can file a flat edge and a smooth curve.

lessons.title: Drilling Holes in Metal
lessons.body:
Drilling holes is essential for bolting, riveting, and fitting parts. You need a drillâeither a hand drill or an electric drill. For accuracy, use a drill press. But in many African workshops, a portable electric drill (500 W to 800 W) is common. Use high-speed steel (HSS) drill bits. For mild steel, a bit with a 118-degree point angle works well. Common sizes: 3 mm, 5 mm, 6.5 mm, 8.5 mm, 10 mm.

First, mark the hole center with a center punch. This prevents the bit from wandering. Apply a few drops of cutting oil (or engine oil) to the punch mark. Start with a small pilot bit (3 mm) to create a guide hole. Then switch to the final size. Run the drill at a moderate speed: for a 6 mm bit in steel, about 600 to 800 RPM. Too fast burns the bit; too slow chips the edge.

Hold the drill perpendicular to the surface. If using a hand drill, use both hands and keep steady pressure. Let the bit cutâdo not force it. Clear chips by withdrawing the bit occasionally. For deep holes, withdraw the bit every few millimeters to clear swarf. Use a brush, not your fingers, to remove chips.

For large holes (over 12 mm), drill a pilot hole first, then use a step drill or a hole saw. For precision, clamp the work to a drill press table. If the bit squeals, reduce speed and add oil. If it smokes, stop and let it cool.

After drilling, deburr the hole with a larger drill bit or a countersink. This removes sharp edges. For tapping (next lesson), the hole size must match the tap. For a 6 mm bolt, drill a 5 mm hole for tapping. Always wear safety glasses. In agriculture, you will drill holes for plow bolts, mower blades, and tool handles. Practice on scrap metal until your holes are straight and clean.

lessons.title: Threading and Tapping
lessons.body:
Threading creates screw threads on a rod (external) or inside a hole (internal). For tool making, you will mostly tap holes to accept bolts. You need a tap set (taper, plug, and bottoming taps) and a tap wrench. For external threads, you need a die and die stock. Common thread sizes: M6, M8, M10, M12. In Africa, both metric and imperial (Whitworth) threads are used. Know which one you need.

To tap a hole, first drill the correct tap drill size. For M6, use a 5.0 mm drill; for M8, 6.8 mm; for M10, 8.5 mm; for M12, 10.2 mm. Clamp the work securely. Start with a taper tap (first tap). Insert it into the hole, keeping it straight. Turn it clockwise with light pressure until it bites. Then turn one full turn forward, then half a turn back to break chips. Apply cutting oil generously.

After the taper tap goes through, use the plug tap (second tap) to cut threads closer to the bottom. For blind holes, use a bottoming tap. Never force a tapâif it binds, back it out, clear chips, and add oil. A broken tap is very difficult to remove.

For external threads, use a die. Clamp the rod in a vise. Chamfer the end with a file. Start the die straight, turn clockwise, and reverse every half turn. Use oil. For a 10 mm rod, you need a 10 mm die. The rod diameter should be slightly less than the die size (e.g., 9.8 mm for M10).

In agriculture, threading is used for bolts, clamps, and adjustable linkages. Practice on scrap metal. Always clean threads with a wire brush. A well-tapped hole holds a bolt securely. Remember: the tap drill size is critical. Too small, and the tap breaks; too large, and the threads strip.

lessons.title: Basic Joining Techniques: Riveting and Bolting
lessons.body:
Joining metal parts is how you assemble tools. Two common methods are riveting and bolting. Riveting is permanent; bolting is removable. For agricultural tools, both are used. You need rivets (solid or blind), a rivet gun or hammer, a bucking bar, and a drill. For bolting, you need bolts, nuts, washers, and wrenches.

For solid riveting, drill a hole slightly larger than the rivet shank (e.g., 4.1 mm for a 4 mm rivet). Insert the rivet through the parts. Place the head on an anvil or bucking bar. Use a ball-peen hammer to flatten the protruding shank into a second head. Start with light taps around the edge, then work toward the center. For a 4 mm rivet, the shank should protrude about 1.5 times the diameter (6 mm).

For blind rivets (pop rivets), use a rivet gun. Drill a hole matching the rivet size. Insert the rivet into the gun, place it in the hole, and squeeze the handle until the mandrel snaps. Blind rivets are fast and work from one side. They are good for sheet metal.

Bolting is stronger and can be disassembled. Use graded bolts (8.8 or 10.9) for high stress. For a 10 mm bolt, drill an 11 mm hole. Place washers under the nut and bolt head. Tighten with a spanner or socket. For vibration, use a lock washer or thread-locking compound. In Africa, many farmers use bolts to attach plow shares, mower blades, and tool handles.

Always match rivet or bolt material to the base metal to avoid galvanic corrosion. Stainless steel rivets in aluminum can cause corrosion. For outdoor tools, use galvanized or stainless bolts. After joining, check that the parts are tight and aligned. Practice on scrap metal until your joints are strong and neat. Remember: a good joint is as strong as the metal around it.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a center punch?
options: B) To create a starting dent for drilling
quiz.explanation: A center punch creates a small dent that guides the drill bit and prevents it from wandering.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to scribe lines on metal?
quiz.explanation: A scriber is a sharp, hardened steel pin used to scratch lines on metal.

quiz.q: What is the recommended TPI for a hacksaw blade when cutting mild steel bar?
quiz.explanation: 18 TPI is a general-purpose blade for mild steel, balancing speed and finish.

quiz.q: When using a hacksaw, pressure should be applied:
quiz.explanation: Applying pressure on the forward stroke cuts efficiently; lifting on return prevents blade wear.

quiz.q: Which snips are used for straight cuts in sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Straight snips have straight blades for cutting straight lines.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of filing metal edges?
options: B) To remove burrs and shape edges
quiz.explanation: Filing removes sharp burrs, squares edges, and shapes metal.

quiz.q: Which file is best for smoothing a curved edge?
quiz.explanation: A half-round file has a curved side for filing curves and a flat side for straight edges.

quiz.q: What is draw filing used for?
quiz.explanation: Draw filing involves pushing the file sideways to create a smooth surface.

quiz.q: What is the correct drill size for tapping an M8 hole?
quiz.explanation: For M8, the tap drill size is 6.8 mm to allow proper thread depth.

quiz.q: Why should you use a pilot hole before drilling a large hole?
options: B) To prevent the drill bit from wandering
D) To make the hole larger
quiz.explanation: A pilot hole guides the larger bit and keeps it centered.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of cutting oil when drilling?
options: B) To cool and lubricate the bit
quiz.explanation: Cutting oil reduces heat and friction, extending drill bit life.

quiz.q: Which tap is used to start a thread in a hole?
quiz.explanation: The taper tap has a long chamfer to start the thread easily.

quiz.q: When tapping, why do you reverse the tap every half turn?
quiz.explanation: Reversing breaks chips and prevents the tap from jamming.

quiz.q: What is the correct tap drill size for an M10 hole?
quiz.explanation: For M10, use an 8.5 mm drill for tapping.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to cut external threads on a rod?
quiz.explanation: A die cuts external threads on a cylindrical rod.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of bolting over riveting?
quiz.explanation: Bolted joints can be taken apart for maintenance or replacement.

quiz.q: What is a bucking bar used for in riveting?
options: A) To hold the rivet head
quiz.explanation: A bucking bar supports the rivet head while you hammer the shank.

quiz.q: How much should a solid rivet shank protrude before hammering?
quiz.explanation: A protrusion of about 1.5 times the diameter allows enough material to form a second head.

quiz.q: What is a blind rivet also known as?
quiz.explanation: Blind rivets are commonly called pop rivets and are set with a rivet gun.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mixing stainless steel rivets with aluminum parts?
options: D) They are hard to install
quiz.explanation: Dissimilar metals can cause galvanic corrosion, especially in outdoor conditions.

quiz.q: What is the first step in measuring and marking out metal?
quiz.explanation: A clean surface ensures that layout dye or marks adhere properly.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to check that an edge is at 90 degrees?
quiz.explanation: A try square is used to check and mark right angles.

quiz.q: What is the recommended file length for general work?
quiz.explanation: A 200 mm file is a versatile size for most bench work.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a file card?
quiz.explanation: A file card is a wire brush used to remove metal chips from file teeth.

quiz.q: When drilling, what should you do if the drill bit squeals?
options: B) Reduce speed and add oil
quiz.explanation: Squealing indicates excessive speed or lack of lubrication; reduce speed and add cutting oil.

quiz.q: What is the correct drill size for a 10 mm bolt hole?
quiz.explanation: For a 10 mm bolt, an 11 mm hole provides clearance for easy insertion.

quiz.q: Which type of tap is used for blind holes?
quiz.explanation: A bottoming tap has a short chamfer to cut threads close to the bottom of a blind hole.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a center punch in drilling?
options: A) To mark the hole location
B) To create a starting point for the drill
C) To measure the hole depth
quiz.explanation: A center punch creates a small indentation that guides the drill bit.

quiz.q: When cutting with tin snips, why should you not close the snips completely?
quiz.explanation: Closing the snips completely can deform the metal and leave a jagged edge.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using a drill press over a hand drill?
quiz.explanation: A drill press holds the bit perpendicular and steady, resulting in more accurate holes.
